questions.question: What are default and static methods in interfaces, and why were they added in Java 8?
questions.title: Default and Static Methods in Interfaces
questions.direct_answer: Default methods allow interfaces to provide a method body using the default keyword, so new methods can be added without breaking all implementing classes. Static methods in interfaces work like regular static utility methods scoped to the interface. Both were added in Java 8 primarily to enable the Collections API to evolve — methods like List.sort() and Collection.stream() are default methods.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand how Java 8 evolved interfaces beyond pure abstraction, the diamond problem resolution rules, and practical implications for API design
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Confusing default methods with abstract methods, or not knowing the resolution rules when two interfaces provide conflicting default methods
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the diamond problem resolution (class wins over interface, sub-interface wins over parent, compiler error if ambiguous — must override), and connect to real JDK examples like Iterable.forEach()

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Default methods = backward-compatible API evolution** — how Java added `Collection.stream()` without breaking every existing implementation.
- **Static methods = utility methods namespaced to the interface** — `List.of()`, `Map.of()`; not inherited by implementing classes.
- **Diamond problem forces override** — two interfaces with same default method: compiler demands explicit `InterfaceName.super.method()`.
- **Resolution order: concrete class wins > sub-interface wins > must override** — in that priority order.
- **Default methods with state = wrong tool** — if your default method needs instance state, it belongs in an abstract class.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Default and static methods in interfaces were added in Java 8 to extend interfaces without breaking every class that implements them — the motivation was adding `Collection.stream()` to millions of existing codebases.

**Default methods:**
- Provide a method body in the interface using the `default` keyword
- Existing implementations automatically inherit the behavior without any code changes
- Classic example: `Collection.stream()` was added as a default — no custom collection broke

**Static methods:**
- Utility methods namespaced to the interface — `List.of()`, `Map.of()`, `Comparator.naturalOrder()`
- Not inherited by implementing classes; called on the interface name directly

**Diamond problem:**
- Two interfaces with the same default method: the compiler forces you to override it
- Resolve with `InterfaceName.super.method()` to explicitly choose which default to use
- Resolution rules: concrete class wins > sub-interface wins > must override if still ambiguous

I recommend default methods for backward-compatible API evolution, not as a way to add implementation inheritance — if your default method needs state, it belongs in an abstract class.

sections.title: Build the mental model
sections.content:
The **diamond problem** is the ambiguity that appears when one type inherits the same method from two paths — which version runs?

Java **forbids multiple inheritance of classes** precisely to avoid this.

With Java 8 default methods in interfaces, the diamond can re-appear, so the compiler **forces you to resolve it explicitly**: if a class inherits conflicting `default` methods from two interfaces, it must **override the method** and can call a specific parent version via `InterfaceName.super.method()`. The rule order: **class wins over interface**, **more specific interface wins over less specific**, and **explicit override is required** otherwise (compile error).

A common mistake is confusing default methods with abstract methods, or not knowing the resolution rules when two interfaces provide conflicting default methods

sections.title: When Two Interfaces Disagree: How Java Forces You to Resolve the Conflict

Important trade-off
sections.content: **Composition**: part created inside owner (`new` in constructor), lifecycle bound — dies with parent. Maps to CASCADE DELETE. **Aggregation**: part passed in externally, outlives owner — Spring `@Autowired` is aggregation. **Association**: objects interact with no ownership (method parameter, local ref). Test: delete the parent — should the child also be deleted? Yes = composition. No = aggregation. No relationship = association.

questions.direct_answer: The **diamond problem** is the ambiguity that appears when one type inherits the same method from two paths — which version runs? Java **forbids multiple inheritance of classes** precisely to avoid this. With Java 8 default methods in interfaces, the diamond can re-appear, so the compiler **forces you to resolve it explicitly**: if a class inherits conflicting `default` methods from two interfaces, it must **override the method** and can call a specific parent version via `InterfaceName.super.method()`. interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands why Java 1.0 banned multiple inheritance of classes, how default methods in Java 8 reintroduced the possibility of a diamond, and what resolution rules the compiler applies
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Claiming Java 'has no diamond problem because there's no multiple inheritance' — ignoring that interfaces with default methods can form a diamond. Forgetting the `Interface.super.method()` syntax to disambiguate

sections.title: Why the "Diamond" — and Why Java Banned It From Day One for Classes
sections.content:
The diamond problem is the inheritance pattern that looks like a diamond: `D` inherits from both `B` and `C`, and both `B` and `C` inherit from `A`. If `A` defines `greet()` and both `B` and `C` override it differently, what should `d.greet()` do? Which version wins — `B`'s or `C`'s? Both? Neither?

C++ allowed this via **multiple class inheritance** and paid for it with virtual inheritance, constructor complexity, and a category of bugs where state was duplicated unexpectedly. Java's designers looked at that mess and made a blunt decision: a class can `extends` exactly one other class. No multiple class inheritance means no diamond at the class level. For behavior sharing across unrelated classes, Java gave you **interfaces** — originally pure contracts with no method bodies, so no ambiguity.

That clean story held until **Java 8** introduced `default` methods on interfaces. Default methods are real method bodies attached to interfaces. The moment a class can implement two interfaces that both define `default greet()`, the diamond is back. Java 8 resolved this by making the compiler **refuse to guess** — you must override and disambiguate manually.

sections.title: The Diamond Shape — Two Paths to the Same Method
The Diamond That Compiles — Until You Try to Call the Method
The Fix — Override and Use `Interface.super.method()`
The Three Resolution Rules the Compiler Actually Applies
Why Java's Choice — Ban First, Allow Later — Pays Off
sections.content:
**Forbid multiple class inheritance:** yes, it's a limitation; C++ programmers coming to Java sometimes complain. But it eliminates virtual-base-class complexity, state duplication, and constructor ordering bugs. The cost is mild — composition covers 90% of what multiple inheritance was used for.

**Allow diamonds on interfaces (Java 8+):** default methods exist specifically to let libraries add methods without breaking every existing implementor. That's how `java.util.Collection` got `stream()` and `forEach()` retroactively. The trade-off: diamonds are back. The mitigation: the compiler forces you to resolve them, so the ambiguity is surfaced at compile time.

**Alternative Java could have taken:** auto-pick one (e.g., declaration order) — rejected because it's fragile; reordering `implements` clauses would change behavior silently. Java's "explicit override" choice is verbose but safe.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Diamond problem** = one type inherits the same method via two paths — which version runs?
- **Java forbids multiple class inheritance** — `extends` takes exactly one class. This eliminates the diamond at the class level.
- **Interfaces with `default` methods (Java 8+) can re-create the diamond** — compiler forces explicit resolution.
- **Three resolution rules:** class wins over interface, more specific interface wins, else explicit override required.
- **Use `Interface.super.method()`** to call a specific parent interface's default from an overriding class.
- **Abstract methods don't diamond** — ambiguity exists only when both parents provide a body.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The diamond problem is the classic multiple-inheritance ambiguity — a type inherits the same method from two parents and the language has to decide which version wins.

**How Java 1.0 handled it**
- Banned multiple class inheritance entirely — a class `extends` exactly one other class
- Interfaces were pure contracts with no method bodies, so no ambiguity even with `implements A, B`
- That eliminated the C++-style diamond by design

**Why it came back in Java 8**
- Default methods let you add real method bodies to interfaces without breaking existing implementors — that's how `Collection.stream()` was added retroactively
- A class implementing two interfaces that both provide a `default` for the same method creates the diamond

**The three resolution rules the compiler applies**
- Class always wins — a concrete method on the class (or any superclass) overrides any interface `default`
- More specific interface wins — if one interface extends the other, the child's default wins
- Otherwise explicit override required — unrelated interfaces both providing a default produce a compile error until you override

**Disambiguation syntax**
- Use `Interface.super.method()` to reach a specific parent interface's body: `return Friendly.super.greet();`
- This keeps resolution explicit in code, not dependent on `implements` order

**Recommendation:** Lean on the compiler — Java catches diamond ambiguities at compile time, so as long as you add an explicit `@Override` whenever the compiler complains, you can't ship a silent ambiguity. Use default methods to add library capabilities retroactively, but keep them few and focused to minimize the diamond surface.

questions.question: Association vs Aggregation vs Composition in Java
questions.title: Association vs Aggregation vs Composition in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Composition**: part created inside owner (`new` in constructor), lifecycle bound — dies with parent. Maps to CASCADE DELETE. **Aggregation**: part passed in externally, outlives owner — Spring `@Autowired` is aggregation. **Association**: objects interact with no ownership (method parameter, local ref). Test: delete the parent — should the child also be deleted? Yes = composition. No = aggregation. No relationship = association.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the lifecycle and ownership differences between the three relationship types — not just UML terminology but how it translates to Java code decisions about object creation and destruction
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating all three as the same thing or confusing aggregation with composition. Giving UML definitions without showing how the distinction appears in actual Java code — specifically who creates the dependent object and what happens when the parent is garbage collected
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show in code how composition means the part is created inside the whole (no independent lifecycle), while aggregation means the part is passed in and survives the whole's destruction. Connect to real Spring patterns — DI is aggregation by default, inner beans are composition

sections.title: The Question Behind the Question: Who Owns the Object's Lifecycle?
sections.content:
Think of a car. The **engine** is composition — the car created it, the car owns it, and when the car is scrapped, the engine goes with it. The **driver** is aggregation — the driver exists independently, gets assigned to the car, and continues to exist after the car is gone. The car's relationship with the **road** is association — they interact but neither owns or manages the other.

These three terms describe the same thing in different strengths: **how tightly one object's lifecycle is bound to another's.** In Java, there's no keyword for any of them — no `aggregates` or `composes` modifier. The distinction lives entirely in how you write the code: who calls `new`, who holds the reference, and what happens when the container object is garbage collected.

The reason interviewers ask this isn't to test UML knowledge. It's to see whether you think about **object ownership** when designing classes. A class that creates its dependencies internally (composition) is tightly coupled — you can't test it without the real dependency. A class that receives its dependencies (aggregation) is loosely coupled — you can inject mocks. This distinction is the foundation of dependency injection, and understanding it at the relationship level makes DI patterns intuitive rather than magical.

sections.title: Three Relationship Types at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Association|~Weakest — uses|no lifecycle ownership|method param / local ref|Teacher ↔ Student
blue|Aggregation|~Medium — has-a shared|part outlives the whole|passed via constructor|Spring @Autowired = aggregation
emerald|Composition|~Strongest — has-a exclusive|part dies with the whole|new inside constructor|CASCADE DELETE in databases
violet|Lifecycle Test|~Delete parent → child too?|Yes = composition|No = aggregation|Neither manages = association

sections.title: Lifecycle Ownership: The One Dimension That Separates All Three
sections.content:
The three relationships form a spectrum from loosest to tightest coupling. The lifecycle column is what actually matters in code.

| Aspect | Association | Aggregation | Composition |
|---|---|---|---|
| Relationship strength | Weakest — uses | Medium — has-a (shared) | Strongest — has-a (exclusive) |
| Lifecycle ownership | Independent — neither manages the other | Part outlives the whole | Part dies with the whole |
| Java pattern | Method parameter or local reference | Field injected via constructor/setter | Field created inside constructor or `new` inline |
| Directionality | Can be bidirectional | Typically unidirectional | Always unidirectional |
| Real-world analogy | Teacher ↔ Student | Department → Professor | House → Room |

The code distinction is concrete. In aggregation, the dependent object is **passed in** — it existed before and will exist after. In composition, the dependent object is **created inside** the owner — its lifecycle is entirely controlled.

This maps directly to Spring's dependency injection model. When Spring injects a bean via `@Autowired`, that's **aggregation** — the bean exists in the container independently, and multiple classes can share it. When you define an inner bean in XML config or create an object with `new` inside a method, that's **composition** — the object lives and dies with its creator.

sections.title: Composition in Code — Owner Creates the Part, Part Dies With It
Aggregation in Code — Part Is Passed In, Outlives the Owner
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Composition** — owner creates the part with `new` in its constructor; delete the owner and the part disappears.
- **Aggregation** — part is passed in from outside and outlives the owner; Spring `@Autowired` is aggregation.
- **Association** — two objects interact but neither owns the other's lifecycle; often just a method parameter.
- **No Java keyword distinguishes them** — the difference is who calls `new` and who holds the reference.
- **Lifecycle test** — delete the parent: if child should go too = composition; if child survives = aggregation.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Association, aggregation, and composition describe three types of relationships between objects in object-oriented design — they differ in how strongly one object's lifecycle is tied to another's. There is no special Java syntax for any of them; the distinction lives entirely in who creates the object and who holds the reference.

**Composition — owns and creates:**
- Composition is the tightest binding: the owner creates the part using `new` directly in its constructor — `Car` does `this.engine = new Engine()`, meaning the car's construction directly causes the engine's creation
- The part cannot exist independently — when `Car` is garbage-collected with no other references to its engine, the engine is collected too; this maps to `CASCADE DELETE` in a relational database
- A real giveaway: if you can't create the part without creating the owner first, it's composition

**Aggregation — uses but doesn't own:**
- Aggregation is a looser relationship: the part is constructed elsewhere and passed in — `Department(List<Professor> professors)` receives professors that were created independently
- Professors continue to exist after the department is dissolved — they were never owned by the department, just referenced; the department going away doesn't trigger their destruction
- Spring `@Autowired` is always aggregation — the beans are created and managed by the container, not by the class that receives them

**Association — interacts without ownership:**
- Association is the loosest: two objects interact but neither creates nor manages the other's lifecycle; the relationship exists only for the duration of an interaction
- This shows up as a method parameter or a temporary local reference — a `Teacher` who grades a `Student` doesn't create the student and doesn't hold a permanent field reference

I recommend the lifecycle test when uncertain: if you delete the parent and the child should disappear with it, that is composition. If the child continues to exist independently, that is aggregation.

questions.question: Enums in Java — More Than Constants
questions.title: Enums in Java — More Than Constants
questions.direct_answer: Java enums are full classes — each constant is a **singleton instance** created at class loading. Constructors are implicitly `private`. Compare with `==` (null-safe, never throws NPE). Constant-specific abstract methods = Strategy pattern without class hierarchy — compiler forces implementation per constant. `EnumSet`/`EnumMap` for collections (faster than HashSet/HashMap). Thread-safe and serialization-safe by design.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows that Java enums are full classes — they can have fields, constructors, methods, and even implement interfaces. The interviewer wants to see if they understand enum's role in replacing integer constants and strategy patterns
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating enums as simple constants like C-style enums. Comparing enum values with equals() instead of == (both work, but == is null-safe and faster). Not knowing that enum constructors are implicitly private and each constant is a singleton instance
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show how enums can implement the Strategy pattern by having each constant override an abstract method. Mention that enums are inherently serialization-safe (no duplicate instance problem), thread-safe (initialized in class loading), and work in switch statements including the newer switch expressions

sections.title: Enums Are Classes — The Feature Most Java Developers Underuse
sections.content:
In most languages, enums are just named integers. Java took a fundamentally different approach: **every enum is a full class** that extends `java.lang.Enum`. Each enum constant is a singleton instance of that class, created once during class loading and never again.

This means enums can have fields, constructors, methods, and implement interfaces — just like any other class. The constructor is implicitly `private` (you can't create enum instances with `new`), and the set of instances is fixed at compile time. These two constraints — private construction and a fixed instance set — give enums properties that are hard to achieve any other way.

Enums are **inherently thread-safe** because the JVM guarantees class loading happens once, in a thread-safe manner. They're **serialization-safe** because deserialization returns the existing singleton rather than creating a new instance — the duplicate-instance problem that plagues `Serializable` classes doesn't exist for enums. And they work natively in `switch` statements, including the newer pattern-matching switch expressions in Java 17+.

The interviewer asking this question wants to know if you see enums as a tool for modeling closed sets of behavior — not just named constants.

sections.title: Enums in Java — Key Concepts
sections.content:
amber|Enum Constants|~Singleton instances|one per constant, created at load|compare with ==, not equals()|private constructor always
blue|Fields + Methods|~Full class capabilities|can implement interfaces|constructors set per-constant state|abstract methods overridden per constant
emerald|Strategy Pattern|~Per-constant behavior|abstract method in enum|each constant provides impl|compiler enforces — no silent gaps
violet|Collections|~EnumSet and EnumMap|bit-vector and array-backed|faster than HashSet/HashMap|EnumSet.allOf(), EnumSet.of()

sections.title: Enums as Strategy: Behavior That Varies by Constant
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Enum constants are singleton instances** — created once at class loading; `new` is impossible; instance set is fixed at compile time.
- **Compare enums with `==`, not `equals()`** — both work; `==` is null-safe and faster for guaranteed singletons.
- **Constant-specific abstract methods replace if-else chains** — new constants must implement at compile time; switches silently ignore new values.
- **Enums are serialization-safe** — deserialization returns the existing singleton; no duplicate-instance problem.
- **`EnumSet`/`EnumMap` for enum collections** — bit-vector and array-backed; faster than `HashSet`/`HashMap`.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java enums aren't named integers — they're full classes where each constant is a singleton instance with its own fields, methods, and interface implementations.

**Why they're more powerful than constants**
- Each constant is a singleton created once at class loading; constructors are implicitly private, so the instance set is fixed at compile time
- Compare with `==`, not `equals()` — both work, but `==` is null-safe and faster for singletons
- Use `EnumSet`/`EnumMap` for collections — bit-vector and array-backed, faster than `HashSet`/`HashMap`

**The strategy pattern without a class hierarchy**
- Define an `abstract` method in the enum and override it per constant: `PREMIUM { public double applyDiscount(double p) { return p * 0.85; } }`
- Adding a new constant forces you to implement the method at compile time — a switch statement would silently ignore new values

**Built-in safety properties**
- Thread-safe: JVM initializes enums during class loading, once, safely
- Serialization-safe: deserialization returns the existing singleton, not a new duplicate — no broken `==` identity

I recommend enums wherever you have a closed fixed set of options with associated behavior — not just as a replacement for integer constants.

questions.question: How do you create an immutable class in Java and why does immutability matter?
questions.title: Immutability in Java — How and Why
questions.direct_answer: An immutable class is one whose state cannot change after construction. To create one: make the class final, make all fields private and final, don't provide setters, perform defensive copies of mutable fields in the constructor and getters, and initialize all fields via the constructor. Immutability matters because immutable objects are inherently thread-safe, safe as HashMap keys, and eliminate entire categories of bugs.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the full recipe for creating immutable objects and the thread-safety benefits
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Declaring fields final but forgetting defensive copies — if a final field holds a reference to a mutable List, the object is NOT truly immutable
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Java records as a modern shortcut, explain the connection between immutability and thread safety, and note that String is the most famous immutable class

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`final` freezes the reference, not the object** — a `final List` can still have elements added; true immutability requires more.
- **Four requirements: `final` class, `private final` fields, no setters, defensive copies** — the defensive copy is the step most people miss.
- **`List.copyOf()` vs `Collections.unmodifiableList()`** — `copyOf()` is independent; `unmodifiableList()` wraps the original so changes leak through.
- **Records handle 3 of 4 automatically** — `final` class, `final` fields, no setters; they do NOT defensively copy mutable components.
- **Immutable objects are inherently thread-safe** — no synchronization needed; safe to share across threads freely.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The trap with immutable classes is that `final` prevents reassignment, not mutation — a `final List<String>` can still have elements added or removed.

**Four requirements for true immutability:**
- Make the class `final` — prevents mutable subclasses from adding state or overriding methods
- All fields `private final` — prevents direct access and reassignment after construction
- No setters or mutation methods — prevents internal state changes
- **Defensive copies** for mutable components — the step most people miss

**Defensive copying:**
- `this.tags = tags` means the caller's list and your internal field share the same object — mutating one mutates both
- `this.tags = List.copyOf(tags)` creates an independent unmodifiable copy — modifications from neither side affect the other
- `Collections.unmodifiableList(tags)` is insufficient — it wraps the original, so changes to the original still leak through

**Records and immutability:**
- Records handle `final` class, `final` fields, and no setters automatically
- Records do **not** defensively copy mutable components — add `Order { items = List.copyOf(items); }` in the compact constructor

I recommend `List.copyOf()` over `Collections.unmodifiableList()` for defensive copies — it provides true independence from the original.
